electrical_safety.name: electrical_safety
electrical_safety.description: Electrical safety refers to the identification, prevention, and control of hazards related to the use and maintenance of electrical systems and equipment in the workplace. It encompasses safe work practices, hazard recognition, and compliance with regulations to prevent electrical injuries, fires, and equipment damage. Observations in this category often involve unsafe wiring, improper use of electrical tools, or lack of protective measures.
examples: Observed missing lockout tag on electrical panel.
Extension cords running across walkways without protection.
Employee using damaged power tool with exposed wires.
No warning signage near high voltage area.
Routine electrical safety inspection completed.

arc_flash.name: arc_flash
arc_flash.description: Arc flash refers to a dangerous release of energy caused by an electrical arc, resulting in intense heat, light, and pressure that can cause severe injuries or fatalities. In HSE, this category covers incidents, near misses, or hazards where workers are exposed to arc flash risks, often during maintenance or operation of electrical equipment. Observations may include inadequate PPE, improper procedures, or lack of arc flash labeling.
examples: Worker entered switchgear room without arc flash PPE.
Arc flash label missing on main distribution panel.
Near miss: arc flash occurred during breaker maintenance.
Observed burn marks from previous arc flash event.
No arc flash boundary marked on electrical cabinet.

fire_risk.name: fire_risk
fire_risk.description: Fire risk involves the potential for ignition, spread, and harm from fire due to electrical faults, flammable materials, or unsafe practices. In HSE, this category includes observations of conditions or behaviors that could lead to fire, such as overloaded circuits, accumulation of combustible dust, or blocked fire exits. It is critical for preventing property damage, injuries, and environmental harm.
examples: Overloaded power strip found behind server rack.
Flammable materials stored near electrical panel.
Fire extinguisher blocked by equipment.
Accumulation of dust in electrical room.
Unattended soldering iron left plugged in.

short_circuit.name: short_circuit
short_circuit.description: Short circuit refers to an unintended connection between two points in an electrical circuit, causing excessive current flow and potential equipment damage, fire, or injury. In HSE, this category covers incidents, hazards, or near misses involving short circuits, often due to faulty wiring, damaged insulation, or improper repairs. Observations may include tripped breakers, burnt smells, or visible sparks.
examples: Breaker tripped due to short circuit in lighting panel.
Burnt smell detected near motor control center.
Observed sparks from junction box during operation.
Short circuit caused power outage in production area.
Damaged cable insulation led to short circuit.

wiring_fault.name: wiring_fault
wiring_fault.description: Wiring fault refers to defects or errors in electrical wiring, such as loose connections, incorrect wiring, or damaged cables, which can lead to equipment failure, fire, or electric shock. In HSE, this category includes observations of improper installations, exposed conductors, or signs of wear and tear in wiring systems. Timely identification is crucial for preventing incidents.
examples: Loose wire connection found in control panel.
Incorrectly wired outlet discovered during inspection.
Damaged insulation on power cable near machine.
Exposed conductor observed in ceiling wiring.
Wiring fault caused intermittent equipment shutdown.

equipment_failure.name: equipment_failure
equipment_failure.description: Equipment failure refers to the malfunction or breakdown of electrical or mechanical devices, which can create safety hazards, disrupt operations, or lead to secondary incidents. In HSE, this category includes reports of failed machinery, tripped systems, or non-functional safety devices, often requiring immediate maintenance or shutdown.
examples: Main generator failed during routine operation.
Emergency stop button not functioning on conveyor.
Pump motor overheated and shut down unexpectedly.
Fire alarm panel displayed equipment fault code.
Lighting system failure in warehouse area.

overload.name: overload
overload.description: Overload refers to a condition where electrical circuits or equipment are subjected to currents or loads beyond their rated capacity, increasing the risk of overheating, fire, or equipment damage. In HSE, this category includes observations of overloaded outlets, excessive use of extension cords, or machinery running above safe limits.
examples: Multiple heaters plugged into single outlet caused overload.
Observed tripped breaker due to circuit overload.
Extension cord used to power several high-wattage devices.
Motor running above rated load for extended period.
Overload warning displayed on control panel.

ground_fault.name: ground_fault
ground_fault.description: Ground fault refers to an unintentional electrical path between a power source and the ground, which can result in electric shock, equipment damage, or fire. In HSE, this category includes incidents or hazards where faulty insulation, damaged equipment, or moisture leads to current leakage to ground.
examples: Ground fault detected on portable generator.
Moisture in panel caused ground fault trip.
Worker received mild shock due to ground fault in tool.
Ground fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) activated in restroom.
Insulation failure led to ground fault in lighting system.

exposed_wiring.name: exposed_wiring
exposed_wiring.description: Exposed wiring refers to electrical conductors that are not properly insulated or covered, posing risks of electric shock, short circuit, or fire. In HSE, this category includes observations of bare wires, damaged cable sheaths, or temporary wiring left unprotected in work areas.
examples: Exposed wires found near loading dock.
Temporary wiring left uncovered in hallway.
Damaged cable sheath exposing conductors.
Bare wires hanging from ceiling light fixture.
Observed uninsulated wiring in maintenance area.

power_outage.name: power_outage
power_outage.description: Power outage refers to the loss of electrical supply to a facility or area, which can disrupt operations, compromise safety systems, and create hazards for workers. In HSE, this category includes both planned and unplanned outages, as well as their impacts on critical equipment and emergency procedures.
examples: Unplanned power outage halted production line.
Backup generator activated during power failure.
Emergency lighting failed to operate during blackout.
Power outage affected fire alarm system.
Planned power shutdown for maintenance announced.

shock_hazard.name: shock_hazard
shock_hazard.description: Shock hazard refers to the risk of electric shock due to contact with live electrical parts, faulty equipment, or improper grounding. In HSE, this category includes observations of unsafe conditions where workers could be exposed to electrical current, such as missing covers, wet environments, or damaged tools.
examples: Missing cover on live electrical panel presents shock hazard.
Wet floor near power outlet increases shock risk.
Damaged extension cord exposes workers to electric shock.
Observed worker using tool with frayed power cord.
Improperly grounded equipment identified as shock hazard.

month.name: month
month.description: In HSE analytics, 'month' refers to a calendar period of approximately 30 days used for tracking, reporting, and analyzing safety and environmental data. Monthly intervals are commonly used to identify trends, monitor compliance, and assess the effectiveness of safety initiatives over time. Observations, incidents, and corrective actions are often aggregated and reviewed on a monthly basis.
examples: Three near misses were reported this month.
Monthly safety inspection completed for March.
Monthly environmental audit identified two minor spills.
No lost time injuries recorded in the last month.
Monthly review of hazard observations shows a decrease.

quarter.name: quarter
quarter.description: In the HSE context, 'quarter' denotes a three-month period used for summarizing and evaluating safety and environmental performance. Quarterly intervals help organizations assess progress on safety goals, review incident rates, and plan corrective actions. Many regulatory and internal reports are structured around quarterly data.
examples: Quarterly safety meeting held to discuss incident trends.
Quarterly report shows a reduction in environmental violations.
No recordable injuries occurred this quarter.
Quarterly review identified recurring housekeeping hazards.
Quarterly audit completed for all work areas.

year.name: year
year.description: In HSE analytics, 'year' refers to a twelve-month period used for comprehensive evaluation of safety and environmental performance. Annual reviews are essential for identifying long-term trends, setting strategic goals, and fulfilling regulatory reporting requirements. Yearly data often includes summaries of incidents, near misses, and compliance activities.
examples: Annual safety report submitted to management.
No fatalities recorded this year.
Yearly review shows improvement in hazard reporting.
Annual environmental compliance audit completed.
Year-end summary highlights reduction in lost time injuries.

week.name: week
week.description: In the HSE domain, 'week' represents a seven-day period used for short-term monitoring and reporting of safety and environmental activities. Weekly intervals are useful for tracking immediate issues, scheduling inspections, and ensuring timely follow-up on hazards or incidents. Many frontline safety observations and toolbox talks are organized on a weekly basis.
examples: Weekly safety walk completed on Friday.
Two near misses reported this week.
Weekly housekeeping inspection found blocked exits.
No environmental incidents recorded this week.
Weekly toolbox talk focused on PPE compliance.

safety_observation.name: safety_observation
safety_observation.description: A safety observation refers to the act of noticing and recording behaviors, conditions, or practices that impact workplace safety, whether positive or negative. In HSE, these observations are used to identify trends, reinforce safe practices, and address unsafe actions before they lead to incidents. They often include both compliance with and deviations from safety protocols.
examples: Observed worker wearing full PPE while operating forklift.
Noted that emergency exit was partially blocked by equipment.
Employee used proper lockout/tagout procedure during maintenance.
Found spill on walkway promptly cleaned up by staff.
Observed unsafe lifting technique in warehouse area.

incident.name: incident
incident.description: An incident in HSE refers to any unplanned event that results in or could result in injury, illness, property damage, or environmental harm. Incidents are formally reported and investigated to determine root causes and prevent recurrence. This category includes accidents, injuries, equipment failures, and other significant safety events.
examples: Worker suffered a laceration to hand while using box cutter.
Forklift collided with storage rack causing minor damage.
Chemical spill resulted in evacuation of production area.
Employee slipped on wet floor and sprained ankle.
Fire alarm triggered due to electrical short in panel.

near_miss.name: near_miss
near_miss.description: A near miss is an unplanned event that did not result in injury, illness, or damage but had the potential to do so. In HSE, near misses are critical for proactive risk management, as they highlight hazards and unsafe conditions before they cause harm. Reporting near misses helps organizations address underlying issues and prevent future incidents.
examples: Falling tool narrowly missed worker below, no injury occurred.
Forklift reversed into aisle but stopped just before hitting pallet.
Employee tripped over loose cable but regained balance.
Chemical container dropped but did not break or spill.
Overhead load swung out of control but was quickly stabilized.

hazard_report.name: hazard_report
hazard_report.description: A hazard report documents the identification of a condition, process, or behavior that poses a risk to health, safety, or the environment. In HSE, these reports are used to flag potential dangers so corrective actions can be taken before an incident occurs. Hazards can include physical, chemical, ergonomic, or environmental risks.
examples: Reported frayed electrical cord in break room.
Identified unguarded moving parts on conveyor belt.
Noted oil spill near loading dock creating slip hazard.
Flagged missing handrail on stairway.
Reported strong chemical odor in storage area.

environmental_observation.name: environmental_observation
environmental_observation.description: An environmental observation involves noting and recording conditions or events that may impact the environment, such as pollution, waste, emissions, or wildlife disturbances. In HSE, these observations help ensure compliance with environmental regulations and promote sustainable practices. They can include both positive and negative environmental behaviors or incidents.
examples: Observed oil sheen on surface water near outfall.
Noted proper segregation of hazardous waste containers.
Reported excessive dust emissions from construction site.
Spotted wildlife nesting near storage tanks.
Identified leaking valve causing minor chemical release.

maintenance_request.name: maintenance_request
maintenance_request.description: A maintenance request is a formal notification submitted to address equipment, facility, or infrastructure issues that may affect safety, health, or operational efficiency. In HSE, timely maintenance requests help prevent unsafe conditions, equipment failures, and potential incidents. These requests can be for repairs, replacements, or preventive maintenance.
examples: Requested repair of faulty emergency stop button on machine.
Submitted work order for leaking pipe in utility room.
Reported broken safety guard on conveyor belt for replacement.
Requested servicing of malfunctioning fire alarm system.
Notified maintenance of flickering lights in stairwell.

production_facility.name: production_facility
production_facility.description: A production facility refers to the main area where manufacturing, processing, or assembly operations take place. In HSE, this location is associated with observations of machinery hazards, process safety, worker exposure to chemicals, and operational incidents. Typical events include equipment malfunctions, unsafe work practices, or environmental releases within the production area.
examples: Oil spill detected near the mixing station in the production facility.
Guard missing on conveyor belt in the main plant floor.
Worker reported excessive noise exposure in the assembly area.
Unlabeled chemical container found in the manufacturing hall.
Slip hazard due to coolant leak on the production line.

office_space.name: office_space
office_space.description: Office space refers to administrative or clerical work areas within an industrial site, such as rooms with desks, computers, and meeting areas. HSE observations here often involve ergonomic risks, fire safety, indoor air quality, and slips, trips, or falls. Incidents may include blocked emergency exits, poor lighting, or electrical hazards.
examples: Loose carpet tile caused a trip hazard in the main office corridor.
Blocked fire extinguisher found in the admin office.
Employee reported eye strain due to poor lighting at workstation.
Overloaded power strip observed under desk in office space.
Unattended coffee spill in the meeting room.

warehouse.name: warehouse
warehouse.description: A warehouse is a storage area for raw materials, finished goods, or equipment, often involving racking systems, forklifts, and loading activities. HSE concerns include manual handling injuries, falling objects, vehicle-pedestrian interactions, and fire risks. Observations may relate to blocked aisles, unsafe stacking, or improper use of lifting equipment.
examples: Pallets stacked above safe height in the warehouse.
Forklift operating without horn in storage area.
Blocked emergency exit in the stockroom.
Spilled oil near loading zone in the warehouse.
Damaged racking observed in inventory area.

outdoor_area.name: outdoor_area
outdoor_area.description: Outdoor area refers to any external space on the industrial site, such as yards, parking lots, walkways, or open storage zones. HSE observations here often involve weather-related hazards, vehicle movement, environmental spills, and slips or trips. Events may include icy walkways, poor lighting, or unsecured materials exposed to wind.
examples: Icy conditions reported on the main walkway outside.
Unsecured gas cylinders found in the yard.
Oil spill observed near the parking lot entrance.
Trip hazard due to uneven pavement in outdoor area.
Poor lighting in external storage zone.

electrical_room.name: electrical_room
electrical_room.description: An electrical room is a dedicated space housing electrical panels, switchgear, transformers, or control cabinets. HSE risks include electrical shock, arc flash, fire hazards, and restricted access. Observations may involve exposed wiring, blocked access to panels, or improper use of personal protective equipment.
examples: Access to electrical room blocked by storage boxes.
Exposed live wires found in the switchgear room.
No arc flash signage on electrical panel door.
Improper PPE used during maintenance in power room.
Fire extinguisher missing from electrical enclosure.

substation.name: substation
substation.description: A substation is a facility or area where electrical voltage is transformed and distributed, often containing high-voltage equipment and transformers. HSE concerns include electrical hazards, unauthorized access, fire risk, and environmental contamination from oil-filled equipment. Observations may relate to damaged fencing, oil leaks, or missing warning signs.
examples: Oil leak detected under transformer in substation.
Unauthorized personnel found inside substation compound.
Damaged fence observed around electrical substation.
Missing high-voltage warning sign at substation gate.
Fire extinguisher not accessible in transformer yard.

workshop.name: workshop
workshop.description: A workshop is an area designated for equipment repair, fabrication, or maintenance activities, often involving tools, machinery, and manual work. HSE issues include hand injuries, machine guarding, housekeeping, and chemical exposure. Observations may include improper tool storage, lack of PPE, or spills of lubricants.
examples: Oil spill on floor in the maintenance workshop.
Bench grinder missing safety guard in repair area.
Tools left scattered on workbench in fabrication shop.
Employee not wearing gloves during equipment repair.
Improper storage of flammable liquids in tool room.

control_room.name: control_room
control_room.description: A control room is a centralized area where operators monitor and manage plant processes, often using computer systems and control panels. HSE concerns include ergonomic risks, fire safety, emergency response readiness, and access control. Observations may involve blocked egress routes, poor lighting, or malfunctioning alarm systems.
examples: Emergency exit blocked in the control room.
Operator reported faulty alarm panel in monitoring room.
Trip hazard due to loose cables in control center.
Fire extinguisher missing from process control room.
Ergonomic assessment requested for operator workstation.

corridor.name: corridor
corridor.description: A corridor is a passageway or hallway connecting different areas within a facility, used for movement of personnel and sometimes equipment. HSE observations focus on slips, trips, falls, emergency egress, and obstruction hazards. Incidents may include wet floors, blocked pathways, or poor lighting.
examples: Wet floor sign missing after cleaning in corridor.
Fire exit route blocked by boxes in hallway.
Poor lighting reported in main passageway.
Trip hazard due to loose cable in access corridor.
Spill observed in connecting corridor near office area.

loading_dock.name: loading_dock
loading_dock.description: A loading dock is a designated area for loading and unloading goods, often involving trucks, forklifts, and pallet jacks. HSE risks include vehicle-pedestrian collisions, falls from height, manual handling injuries, and pinch points. Observations may relate to unsecured dock plates, poor housekeeping, or lack of traffic controls.
examples: Dock plate not secured during unloading at loading dock.
Pedestrian walkway not marked in shipping dock area.
Pallets blocking emergency exit in loading bay.
Forklift reversing without spotter at receiving dock.
Spill of hydraulic fluid on dock platform.
